q: Why can an array return its 500,000th element as quickly as its first?
options: The array keeps a hidden hash table from each index to its element
Its address is the start address plus the index times the element size
The runtime scans from both ends at once, which halves the work
It is not as quick: reading element i walks past the i elements before it
why: Array elements sit next to each other and all have the same size, so the position of element i is one multiplication and one addition away. No other element has to be visited.
wrong: No extra table is needed; the address is computed with arithmetic.
Scanning from both ends would still be O(n). Arrays do not scan at all to reach an index.
That is how a linked list behaves. An array jumps straight to the computed address.

q: A singly linked list holds n items. What does reading the item at index i cost, and why?
options: O(1): every node stores its own index, so the list can jump to it
O(log n): the list is split in half repeatedly, like binary search
O(i): it follows next pointers from the head one node at a time
O(1) on average, because the nodes are usually stored next to each other
why: Nodes can live anywhere in memory, and each node only knows where the next one is. To reach index i you start at the head and follow i links, which is O(n) in the worst case.
wrong: A stored index does not help: there is still no way to jump to a node without following links.
Binary search needs to jump to the middle in O(1), which a linked list cannot do.
Nothing guarantees the nodes are adjacent, and even if they were, the list has no address formula to use.

q: You insert many items at the front of a sequence that already holds n items. What does each insert cost in a dynamic array and in a linked list?
options: Array O(n), since every item shifts one slot; linked list O(1)
Both O(1), because the front of the sequence is always known
Array O(1) amortized, like append; linked list O(n)
Both O(n), because each insert must first search for its position
why: An array keeps items in consecutive slots, so making room at index 0 moves all n items. A linked list only creates a node and points it at the old head.
wrong: Knowing where the front is does not help the array: its items still have to move to make room.
Amortized O(1) is for adding at the end. Adding at the front of an array shifts everything.
Inserting at the front needs no search; the position is index 0.

q: You look up a value in an array of n numbers. What does the lookup cost if the array is sorted, and if it is not?
options: Both O(n): sorting only helps when the array is printed
Sorted: O(1), since the position of a value follows from its size
Sorted: O(log n) by binary search; unsorted: O(n)
Both O(log n), because binary search works on any array
why: Sorting lets each comparison rule out half of the remaining range. Without order, a slot you have not checked could still hold the value, so the worst case reads all n.
wrong: Sorting is what makes binary search possible, so it does speed up lookups.
Values are not spread evenly, so you cannot compute a value's index directly.
Binary search on unsorted data can discard the half that holds the value and miss it.

q: In a doubly linked list of n nodes you already hold a reference to a node in the middle. What does removing that node cost?
options: O(n): the list must be walked from the head to find the node first
O(log n): the list is halved until the node is reached
O(1): point its previous and next neighbours at each other
O(n): every later node shifts one position to the left
why: The node knows both neighbours, so removing it is two pointer updates. No other node moves and nothing is searched.
wrong: You already hold the node, so there is nothing to find.
Linked lists cannot be halved quickly, and here no search is needed at all.
Shifting happens in arrays. List nodes stay where they are; only links change.

q: A friend says insertion into a linked list is O(1). You must insert a value into a sorted singly linked list of n nodes and keep it sorted. What is the real cost?
options: O(1), because inserting into a linked list is always O(1)
O(log n), by binary searching for the position
O(n log n), because the list is sorted again after the insert
O(n): the walk to the spot dominates the O(1) splice
why: The O(1) claim covers relinking once you stand at the right node. Getting there in a sorted list means walking from the head, which is O(n) in the worst case.
wrong: That ignores the search. The O(1) part starts only after the position is known.
Binary search needs O(1) access to the middle, which a linked list does not have.
Inserting at the right spot keeps the list sorted, so no re-sort is needed.

q: a and b are Python lists with n items each. What does this print, and how does its running time grow with n?
options: [3, 4], in O(n) time: x in b is one built-in call, so it is O(1)
[3, 4], in O(n^2) time: each x in b scans the list b
[3, 4], in O(n log n) time: x in b uses binary search
[3, 4], in O(n) time: the scan stops as soon as x is found
why: The for loop runs n times, and x in b on a list compares x with the items of b one by one, up to n of them. Turning b into a set first makes each check O(1) on average and the whole function O(n).
wrong: One line of code is not one step. For a list, in is a linear scan.
Python cannot assume a list is sorted, so in scans from the start.
Stopping early helps only on hits. Values that are not in b, like 1 and 2, scan all of b.

q: You remove one given value from an unsorted array of n items and must keep the order of the rest. What is the cost?
options: O(n^2): every shifted item needs its own scan
O(1): deleting is just marking the slot as empty
O(log n): binary search finds the value and then it is removed
O(n): one O(n) scan, then one O(n) shift
why: Two linear steps done in sequence add up to O(n + n), which is still O(n). Costs multiply only when one step runs inside the other.
wrong: The scan happens once, before the shift. Sequential steps add, they do not multiply.
Marking leaves a hole, which breaks the order and the array's size. The task asks to keep the rest in order.
The array is unsorted, so binary search cannot find the value, and the shift is O(n) anyway.

q: A game keeps active enemies in a dynamic array, and their order does not matter. How can it remove the enemy at index i in O(1)?
options: Move the last element into slot i, then drop the last slot
Shift every later element one slot to the left
Set slot i to null and leave it there
Copy the array into a linked list, then unlink the node in O(1)
why: Removing the last element of a dynamic array is O(1) and moves nothing. Since order does not matter, filling the gap with the last element avoids shifting the items after i.
wrong: That keeps order but costs O(n), and order was not needed here.
The array keeps a hole, so every loop must skip nulls and the array never shrinks.
The copy alone is O(n), so the removal is not O(1).

q: n numbers arrive one at a time and are kept in a sorted array. Each insert binary searches for its spot and then shifts to make room. What is the total cost for all n?
options: O(n^2): each search is O(log n), but each shift is O(n)
O(n log n): binary search makes each insert O(log n)
O(n): inserts into an array are amortized O(1), like append
O(log n) in total: each insert only needs a position, not a scan
why: Each insert pays two costs: O(log n) to find the spot and up to O(n) to shift the items after it. The shift dominates, so n inserts cost O(n^2) in the worst case. Fast search does not make the move cheap.
wrong: Binary search finds the position, but the items after it still have to move one slot each.
Amortized O(1) holds only for adding at the end, where nothing shifts.
Every insert does at least some work, so n inserts cannot cost less than O(n).

q: Why is looking up a key in a hash map O(1) on average?
options: The keys are kept sorted, so the map binary searches them
The map caches recent lookups, so repeated keys are fast
The hash picks the bucket directly, and buckets stay small
The searched key is compared with every key at the same time
why: The hash function turns the key into a bucket index, so the map goes straight to one bucket. With a good hash and a table that grows as it fills, each bucket holds only a few entries to compare.
wrong: Sorted keys and binary search would give O(log n). A hash map does not keep keys in order.
Caching is not the mechanism. A key looked up for the first time is still O(1) on average.
Comparing with every key is O(n) work; a hash map avoids most of those comparisons.

q: In a hash map that uses separate chaining, two different keys hash to the same bucket. What happens?
options: The second key overwrites the first, since the bucket is taken
The insert fails with an error until the table is resized
The table doubles at once so that the two keys separate
Both are kept in that bucket, and lookups compare the keys
why: A collision is normal. With chaining, each bucket holds a small list of entries. A lookup goes to the bucket and compares the actual keys to find the right one.
wrong: Only an equal key replaces a value. A different key with the same bucket is added next to it.
Collisions are expected, so the map handles them instead of failing.
Resizing depends on how full the table is, not on a single collision, and the keys may still share a bucket.

q: A bad hash function sends every key to the same bucket of a chaining hash map whose chains are plain linked lists. What does a lookup cost now?
options: O(1): hashing still finds the right bucket directly
O(log n): entries in a bucket are kept sorted
Lookups fail, because a bucket cannot hold more than one entry
O(n): the one bucket holds all n entries
why: The O(1) average depends on keys spreading across buckets. When they all collide, the map becomes a single linked list, and a lookup compares keys one at a time.
wrong: Finding the bucket is fast, but searching inside it is now O(n).
Plain chains are unsorted lists, so they are searched from start to end.
A chain can grow to any length; it just gets slow.

q: This Python code tries to use a list as a dictionary key. What does it print?
options: stored, then 1
TypeError, then 0
stored, then 2
TypeError, then 1
why: A dict key must be hashable, and lists are not, because their contents can change. The assignment raises TypeError before anything is stored, so the dict stays empty.
wrong: Lists are not hashable, so the assignment raises TypeError.
A list is never split into separate keys, and here it is not stored at all.
The error is raised before the entry is added, so nothing is stored.

q: Python accepts a tuple of ints as a dict key but rejects a list. What is the reason?
options: Lists can be very long, which makes hashing them too slow
Tuples are kept sorted, so they compare faster
A key's hash must not change while stored, and a list can
Lists are stored by reference and tuples by value
why: The map files each entry under its key's hash. If the key changed after insertion, its hash would change too, and lookups would search the wrong bucket. Tuples of ints cannot change, so their hash is stable.
wrong: Tuples can be just as long. The issue is that a list can change, not its length.
Tuples keep the order you give them; nothing is sorted.
Both are objects accessed by reference in Python. The difference is mutability.

q: A Java list is added to a HashSet and then changed. What does this print?
options: true 1
false 0
false 1
An exception: the set detects that one of its keys changed
why: A List's hashCode is computed from its contents. After key.add(3), the hash no longer matches the bucket where the entry was stored, so contains looks in the wrong place. The entry is still in the set, just unreachable by lookup.
wrong: The set does not re-hash keys when they change, so the lookup uses a new hash and misses.
Changing the key does not remove the entry; size() still counts it.
Sets do not watch their keys. The change goes unnoticed, which is why mutable keys are risky.

q: Point overrides equals() to compare x and y but does not override hashCode(). Two equal Points are added to a HashSet. What does this print?
options: Compile error: equals() needs a matching hashCode()
An exception on the second add, since sets reject duplicates
why: A HashSet first uses hashCode() to pick a bucket and only then calls equals(). The default hashCode() is almost always different for two separate objects, so the second Point is filed elsewhere and never compared. Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
wrong: equals() is consulted only for entries with the same hash, and these two objects have different default hash codes.
The compiler does not enforce the contract. Breaking it compiles and fails at run time.
Sets never throw on duplicates; add() just returns false for a real duplicate.

q: When a hash map's bucket array fills up, it allocates a bigger array. Why can it not just copy the old buckets into the first half?
options: The bucket index depends on the table size, so many entries move
Entries are sorted during a resize, so they must be moved
The key's hash value changes after a resize, so it is computed again
Copying blocks of memory is not allowed for map entries
why: The bucket is computed from the hash and the current size, for example hash mod size. Once the size changes, an entry's correct bucket usually changes too, so each one is placed again. That is O(n), but it happens rarely.
wrong: Hash maps do not sort entries; they only place them by bucket.
The hash comes from the key and does not change. What changes is how it maps to a bucket.
Copying is allowed. It would just leave entries in buckets that lookups would no longer check.

q: Three names are added to a Python dict, then the value for "ada" is updated. What does this print?
options: ['ada', 'kim', 'lee']
['kim', 'ada', 'lee']
['kim', 'lee', 'ada']
The order changes from run to run, since it follows the hash values
why: A Python dict remembers the order in which keys were first inserted. Updating the value of an existing key keeps its place. Insertion order is not sorted order; for that, sort the keys.
wrong: A dict does not sort its keys. It keeps the order they were first added.
Updating an existing key changes its value but not its position.
That is true of sets of strings, not of dicts, which keep insertion order.

q: A server stores user-sent strings as keys of a hash map. An attacker sends many different keys that all land in the same bucket. What happens to the map?
options: The map rejects the keys once a bucket gets too long
A resize spreads the keys out again, so the slowdown is brief
Lookups and inserts degrade to O(n) as one bucket fills up
Not much, since hash map lookups and inserts are always O(1)
why: All crafted keys land in one bucket, so each insert or lookup scans it: O(n) per operation and about O(n^2) for n requests. Runtimes such as Python defend against this with a secret random seed for string hashes in each process.
wrong: A plain hash map has no such limit; it keeps accepting keys and gets slower.
Keys with the same hash land in the same bucket at any table size.
O(1) is the average when keys spread out. When every key shares one bucket, each operation scans it.

q: Appending to an ArrayList or a Python list is called amortized O(1). What does that mean?
options: A rare O(n) copy averages out to O(1) per append
Every single append is O(1), because the array never copies
Appends are O(n), because an append can trigger a copy
On random input, an append is usually O(1)
why: When the array is full, it moves everything to a bigger buffer, which is O(n). Because the capacity grows by a factor, this happens rarely enough that the total over n appends is O(n), so O(1) per append.
wrong: Copies do happen when the array is full; they are just rare.
One expensive append does not make all appends expensive. The cost is averaged over the sequence.
Amortized is not about random input. It is a guaranteed average over any sequence of operations.

q: Why does a dynamic array grow by doubling its capacity instead of adding 10 slots each time it fills up?
options: Doubling uses less memory than adding a fixed number of slots
With +10, n appends copy O(n^2) items; doubling copies O(n)
Both are amortized O(1); doubling just has smaller constants
The capacity must stay a power of two for indexing to work
why: With +10, a full copy happens every 10 appends, and copies get longer as the array grows, adding up to O(n^2). With doubling, the copies are 1, 2, 4 and so on, which sum to less than 2n.
wrong: Doubling can leave up to half the buffer unused; it trades memory for speed.
Fixed growth makes each append O(n) on average, not O(1).
Indexing works with any size; it is just base plus index times size.

q: Summing n ints is O(n) for an array and for a linked list, yet the array is often several times faster. Why?
options: Summing a linked list is really O(n log n)
Arrays are summed in parallel on all CPU cores by default, lists are not
The list is copied into an array before it is summed
Array items are adjacent, so the CPU cache serves most reads
why: Big-O hides constant factors. The CPU loads memory in blocks, so an array's next items are usually already in the cache. List nodes can be scattered, and each step follows a pointer to a new place in memory.
wrong: Each node is visited once, so it is O(n). The difference is in the constant factor.
A plain loop runs on one core. The speedup comes from the cache, not from threads.
No copy is made. The list is walked node by node.

q: In which situation does a linked list beat a dynamic array?
options: Many reads by index, such as items[i] inside a loop
Binary search over data that is kept sorted
Many inserts and removals at nodes you already hold
Tight memory, since nodes store only their values
why: With a reference to the node, a list inserts or removes by changing a few pointers, while an array shifts every later item. For index access, binary search and memory use, the array wins.
wrong: Index access is O(1) in an array and O(n) in a list.
Binary search needs to jump to the middle, which a list cannot do quickly.
Each node also stores at least one pointer, so a list uses more memory per item.

q: This loop removes every 2 from a Python list while iterating over it. What does it print?
options: RuntimeError: the list changed size during iteration
why: The for loop walks by index. Removing the first 2 at index 1 shifts the second 2 into index 1, and the loop moves on to index 2 and never sees it. Build a new list instead, for example with a comprehension.
wrong: That is the intended result, but the shift after each removal makes the loop skip an item.
Python raises that for dicts and sets. Lists allow it and silently skip items.
remove() changes the same list the loop is reading; the loop does not work on a copy.

q: In a singly linked list you hold a reference to node X and want to unlink X. What makes this harder than in a doubly linked list?
options: A node cannot be removed from a singly linked list at all
The node before X must be updated, and only a walk finds it
Every node after X must have its stored index updated
Nothing: setting X to null is enough to remove it from the list
why: Unlinking X means the previous node must skip over it. A singly linked node has no pointer back, so you walk from the head to find the predecessor, which is O(n).
wrong: It can; you just need the previous node first.
List nodes do not store indexes, so nothing after X changes.
That changes only your local variable. The previous node still points at X.

q: This function is meant to reverse a linked list 1 -> 2 -> 3. What does it print?
options: 3 <__main__.Node object at ...>
It never ends, because two nodes keep pointing at each other
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'next'
1 None
why: head.next is overwritten with prev before the old next is saved. The tuple then reads the new head.next, which is None, so the loop stops after one node and the rest of the list is lost. Save nxt = head.next first.
wrong: That would be a correct reversal, but the link to node 2 is overwritten before it is saved.
The loop ends quickly: head becomes None after the first pass.
The loop checks while head before reading head.next, so None is never used as a node.

q: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full. About how many element copies do resizes cause in total for 1,000,000 appends?
options: Fewer than 2,000,000: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... stays under twice the final size
About 20,000,000: about 20 resizes, each copying up to 1,000,000 items
About 500,000,000,000: each append copies everything before it
Zero, because the array always extends in place in memory
why: Each resize copies the current items: 1, 2, 4, up to about 500,000. This series sums to less than twice the last term, so total copying is O(n) and each append is O(1) amortized.
wrong: Only the last resize copies that many. Earlier ones copy half, a quarter and so on.
That is growing by one slot each time. Doubling makes resizes rare.
The memory after the buffer may be in use, so a resize normally moves everything.

q: An editor's undo must reverse the most recent change first, then the one before it. Which structure fits the history of changes?
options: A queue, so changes are undone in the order they were made
A hash map from change id to change, for O(1) access to any change
A stack: push each change, and undo pops the latest
A min-heap keyed by the time of each change
why: Undo is last in, first out: the change made last is undone first. A stack gives exactly that with O(1) push and pop.
wrong: A queue is first in, first out, so it would undo the oldest change first.
A map can find any change quickly, but it does not track which one is the latest.
A min-heap returns the smallest time first, which is the oldest change.

q: This function checks whether brackets are balanced using a stack. What does it print?
options: True False
False True
True True
False False
why: In "([)]" the ) arrives while [ is on top of the stack, so the pair does not match. In "(()" every closer matches, but one ( is left on the stack at the end, and return not stack catches that.
wrong: "([)]" has as many closers as openers, but order matters: ) cannot close the [ opened after it.
The final check returns False when openers are left on the stack, as in "(()".
Both strings fail: one closes in the wrong order and the other leaves a bracket open.

q: Python code implements a queue with list.append() and list.pop(0). Why does a reviewer suggest collections.deque instead?
options: Lists are not thread-safe, and that is the only difference
pop(0) shifts every other item; deque.popleft() is O(1)
pop(0) on an empty list returns None, which hides bugs
A list cannot grow past a fixed size, so the queue would fill up
why: A list is a dynamic array, so taking from the front moves all other items one slot, which is O(n). A deque supports O(1) appends and pops at both ends.
wrong: The main gain is speed: pop(0) is O(n) on a list and popleft() is O(1).
pop(0) on an empty list raises IndexError, and so does popleft() on an empty deque.
Python lists grow as needed. The problem is the cost of removing from the front.

q: A queue uses two stacks: enqueue pushes onto In; dequeue pops from Out, first moving everything from In to Out if Out is empty. What does dequeue cost over many operations?
options: Amortized O(1): each item moves from In to Out at most once
O(n) for every dequeue, since it moves everything between stacks
O(log n), because the stacks keep the items sorted
It cannot work: stacks reverse the order, so items come out LIFO
why: One dequeue can move many items, but each item is pushed onto In once, moved once and popped from Out once. Spread over all operations, that is O(1) per item. The two reversals also keep FIFO order.
wrong: The move only happens when Out is empty. Most dequeues just pop.
The stacks are not sorted; they only reverse the order once.
Reversing twice restores the original order, so items leave FIFO.

q: A fixed-size queue lives in an array with a head index and a tail index that wrap around to 0 at the end. Why wrap instead of shifting items left after each dequeue?
options: Wrapping keeps the items in sorted order
Arrays do not allow items to be moved
Moving the head is O(1), and freed front slots get reused
Wrapping lets the queue hold more items than the array has slots
why: Dequeue just advances the head index. Without wrapping, the tail would run off the end while free slots sit at the start; shifting would fix that but make each dequeue O(n).
wrong: A queue keeps arrival order; wrapping has nothing to do with sorting.
Items can be moved; it is just O(n) per dequeue.
The capacity is still the array size. Wrapping only reuses slots.

q: The same three numbers are added to a deque used as a queue and to a list used as a stack. What does this print?
code:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
s = []
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    q.append(x)
    s.append(x)
print(q.popleft(), s.pop())
why: A queue is first in, first out, so popleft() returns 1, the first number added. A stack is last in, first out, so pop() returns 3, the last number added.
wrong: That swaps the two: the queue gives the oldest item and the stack the newest.
pop() on a list removes from the end, so the stack returns the last item, 3.
popleft() removes from the front of the deque, which holds the first item, 1.

q: To find the next warmer day for each day, a solution loops over the days with a stack and, inside the loop, pops while the top is colder. What is its running time?
options: O(n): each day is pushed once and popped at most once
O(n^2), since there is a loop inside a loop
O(n log n), because the stack is kept sorted with binary search
O(n^2): one day can pop up to n earlier days, and that can happen at every step
why: The inner while loop can run many times in one step, but every pop removes a day that never comes back. Across the whole run there are at most n pushes and n pops.
wrong: Nested loops are not always O(n^2). Count the total work: each item is popped at most once.
The stack is only pushed and popped at the top; no binary search is used.
One step can pop many days, but across the whole run there are at most n pops, because each day is pushed once. The bound comes from the total, not from each step.

q: Which rule defines a binary search tree?
options: Each node's left child is smaller than the node, and its right child is larger
Left subtree keys are all smaller than the node, right subtree keys all larger
Each parent is smaller than both of its children
Every leaf is at the same depth, so the tree is balanced
why: The rule covers whole subtrees, not only direct children. That is what lets a search discard one side at every step and what makes an in-order walk come out sorted.
wrong: Checking only direct children is not enough; a deeper node on the wrong side breaks searches.
That is the min-heap property, which does not support searching by key.
Balance is about height. A BST can be unbalanced and still follow the ordering rule.

q: This function checks that a tree is a BST by comparing each node with its children. What does it print for this tree, and is the tree a BST?
options: False, because 12 is greater than 10
True, but it is not a BST: 12 is in the left subtree of 10
True, and the tree is a valid BST, since every pair is in order
False, because 5 has no left child
why: Every parent-child pair is in order (5 < 12, 5 < 10, 10 < 15), so the check passes. But 12 sits in 10's left subtree, where all keys must be smaller than 10, so a search for 12 from the root would go right and miss it.
wrong: The function never compares 12 with 10; it only compares a node with its direct children.
The BST rule covers whole subtrees, and 12 breaks it under 10.
Missing children are allowed; the function returns True for None.

q: Keys 8, 3, 10, 1, 6 are inserted in that order into an empty BST. What does an in-order traversal print?
why: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. With the BST rule, that always produces keys in ascending order, whatever order they were inserted in.
wrong: That is the insertion order, which here also matches level order. In-order goes left, node, right.
That is pre-order: the node is printed before its subtrees.
That is post-order: the node is printed after both subtrees.

q: Keys 1 to n are inserted in increasing order into a plain BST with no balancing. What does a search cost afterwards?
options: O(log n), as with every binary search tree
O(1), because the largest key ends up at the root
O(n log n), since each level must be sorted again
O(n): the tree becomes one long chain
why: A BST search costs O(height). Sorted inserts always go right, so the tree has height n and behaves like a linked list. Balanced trees fix this by keeping the height near log n.
wrong: O(log n) needs a balanced tree. The shape depends on the insert order.
The first key inserted, 1, is the root, and nothing moves it.
Nothing is sorted during a search; the cost is the length of one path.

q: Orders are looked up by timestamp, and you also need all orders between two timestamps. Which map fits better, and why?
options: A HashMap, since O(1) lookups beat O(log n) for every kind of query
A HashMap: it returns its keys in timestamp order, so ranges work too
A TreeMap, because it inserts in O(1), faster than a HashMap
A TreeMap: sorted keys make a range one O(log n) seek plus a walk
why: A balanced BST finds the start of the range in O(log n) and then walks forward in order. A hash map scatters keys, so a range query has to check every entry. The price is O(log n) lookups instead of O(1) on average.
wrong: O(1) applies to single-key lookups. A hash map has no fast way to answer a range.
A HashMap iterates in an order that depends on hashes, not on key order.
TreeMap inserts are O(log n). The win is ordering, not insert speed.

q: A balanced BST holds about 1,000,000 keys. About how many comparisons does a search need in the worst case?
options: About 1,000, which is the square root of the number of keys
About 20, because the height is about log2 of 1,000,000
About 500,000, half the keys on average
One, because a key leads straight to its node
why: Each level of a balanced tree roughly doubles the number of nodes, so a million keys fit in about 20 levels. A search does one comparison per level.
wrong: Square roots come from other structures. A balanced binary tree halves the range per step.
That is a linear scan. A BST discards a whole subtree at each step.
That is the idea of a hash map. A BST compares its way down from the root.

q: In C, each node of a tree must be freed, and a node's children must be freed before the node itself. Which traversal fits?
options: Pre-order: free the node, then its subtrees
In-order: free the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree
Level order: free the root, then each level below it
Post-order: free both subtrees, then the node
why: Post-order handles a node only after its subtrees. If the node were freed first, its child pointers would be gone or invalid, and the subtrees would leak or be read from freed memory.
wrong: This frees each node before its children, the opposite of the rule, and loses its child pointers unless they are saved.
This frees each node before its right subtree, which breaks the rule.
Like pre-order, this frees every parent before its children.

q: You must print a tree level by level: the root, then all nodes at depth 1, then depth 2. Which approach fits?
options: Recursive in-order traversal
A stack, since DFS reaches every level
A queue: dequeue a node, enqueue its children
Pre-order traversal, then sort the output by value
why: A queue hands out nodes in the order they were found, and nodes are found level by level, so every node at depth d comes out before any at depth d + 1. This is breadth-first search on a tree.
wrong: In-order follows key order, so it mixes nodes from different levels.
A stack goes deep along one branch before visiting the rest of a level.
Values say nothing about depth, so sorting them does not group by level.

q: Sorted input made a plain BST into a chain. A teammate now shuffles the keys randomly before inserting them. What changes?
options: Height is O(log n) on average; in-order output stays sorted
The height becomes exactly log2(n), as in a balanced tree
Nothing changes, because a BST's shape depends only on its keys
Searches get faster, but in-order output is now shuffled too
why: The shape of a plain BST depends on insert order, and random order gives height about O(log n) with high probability, though not a guarantee. In-order output depends only on the BST rule, so it stays sorted.
wrong: Random order makes a short tree likely, not certain. Only balancing guarantees the height.
Shape depends on insert order: the same keys can form a chain or a bushy tree.
In-order output is sorted for any valid BST, whatever its shape.

q: Five numbers are pushed onto a heap with Python's heapq. What does this print?
code:
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 4, 2, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
print(h[0], h == sorted(h))
options: 1 False
1 True
5 False
3 False
why: heapq is a min-heap, so h[0] is always the smallest item. The rest of the list only satisfies parent <= children; here it is [1, 2, 4, 5, 3], which is not sorted.
wrong: A heap guarantees only that each parent is no larger than its children, not that the whole list is sorted.
heapq is a min-heap, so the smallest item is at index 0.
The last item pushed sifts up only while it is smaller than its parent; the top is the minimum.

q: A binary min-heap holds n items. What do peek at the minimum, insert and remove the minimum cost?
options: O(1), O(log n), O(log n)
O(log n), O(log n), O(n)
why: The minimum is always at the root, so peeking is O(1). Insert and remove move one item up or down a path of a complete tree, whose height is about log n.
wrong: Insert and remove must restore the heap order along a path of length log n.
Insert does not shift items like a sorted array; it sifts one item up a single path.
The minimum is at the root, so peek is O(1), and removal sifts down one path, O(log n).

q: How long does it take to check whether some value x is anywhere in a min-heap of n items?
options: O(log n), by walking down from the root as in a BST
O(n): x could be in any branch of the heap
O(1), since a heap is stored in an array
O(log n), by binary searching the underlying array
why: A heap does not say whether x is in the left or the right branch, so a search cannot discard half of the items. It can skip a subtree only when its root is already larger than x, and in the worst case it checks every item.
wrong: A heap has no left-smaller, right-larger rule, so there is no single path to follow.
Being an array gives fast access by index, not by value.
The array is not sorted, so binary search can give wrong answers.

q: You need the 10 largest numbers from a stream of 10 million, with little memory. Which approach fits?
options: Push everything into a max-heap, then pop 10 times
A max-heap of size 10, popping the largest when it passes 10 items
Sort the whole stream and take the last 10
A min-heap of size 10, replacing its minimum when beaten
why: The min-heap holds the 10 largest seen so far, with the weakest of them on top, so each new number is compared with that one. Memory stays at 10 items and the time is O(n log 10), which is close to O(n).
wrong: This gives the right answer but stores all 10 million numbers, which breaks the memory limit.
Popping the largest keeps the 10 smallest numbers instead.
Sorting needs the whole stream in memory and costs O(n log n).

q: A min-heap and a balanced BST can both return the smallest item. Why is a heap the usual choice for a plain priority queue?
options: It is a compact array with O(1) peek and no full ordering
A heap finds any item in O(log n), which a BST cannot
A heap keeps all items sorted, so iterating over it is cheap
A BST needs O(n) to find its minimum
why: A priority queue only needs insert, peek and remove-min. A heap does that in a compact array without pointers. A balanced BST keeps full order, which costs more memory and work for no gain here.
wrong: Searching a heap for an arbitrary item is O(n); the BST is the one with O(log n) search.
A heap is only partly ordered; iterating gives no sorted order.
In a balanced BST the minimum is the leftmost node, found in O(log n).

q: A binary heap with the root at index 0 is stored in a plain array with no child pointers. How does code find a node's children?
options: The array is sorted, so the next slots hold the children
Each slot stores the indexes of its two children next to the value
The tree is complete, so node i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2
Each node's hash gives the slot of its children
why: A heap fills each level from left to right with no gaps. That fixed shape lets index arithmetic replace pointers: children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent at (i - 1) // 2.
wrong: The array is not sorted; positions come from the complete tree shape.
No extra indexes are stored; they are computed from i.
There is no hashing in a heap, only arithmetic on positions.

q: You merge k sorted lists with n items in total, using a min-heap that holds the current head of each list. What is the tightest bound on the total cost?
options: O(n log n), because every item passes through a heap
O(n log k): each item enters and leaves a heap of size at most k
O(nk), because each step compares the current heads of all k lists
O(k log n), because only k items are ever in the heap
why: Each of the n items is pushed once and popped once, and the heap holds at most k items, one per list, so each push or pop is O(log k). Comparing all k heads at every step instead would cost O(nk).
wrong: The heap holds at most k items, not n, so its operations cost O(log k).
That is merging without a heap. The heap finds the smallest head in O(log k).
Every one of the n items is pushed and popped, so the cost grows with n.

q: A social network has 1,000,000 users with about 200 friends each. Should the friendships be stored as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix?
options: A matrix, because checking one friendship is O(1)
A matrix, because an undirected graph only needs half of the matrix
Either one, since both store the same edges
An adjacency list, which stores only the existing friendships
why: A list stores only existing edges, about 200 million entries here. A matrix needs a cell for every pair of users, a trillion cells, almost all empty.
wrong: Fast edge checks do not help if the matrix does not fit in memory.
Half of a trillion cells is still far more than the list needs.
They hold the same edges, but the matrix also spends a cell on every missing edge.

q: When is an adjacency matrix a good choice for a graph?
options: A small or dense graph with many is-there-an-edge checks
A sparse graph, because a matrix saves memory
Code that often loops over the neighbours of every node in turn
Any directed graph, since lists cannot store direction
why: A matrix answers whether u and v are connected in O(1), and its O(V^2) memory is acceptable when V is small or most pairs are connected anyway.
wrong: A matrix always uses V^2 cells, which wastes the most memory when edges are few.
Finding a node's neighbours in a matrix reads a whole row, O(V), even if the node has only two.
Adjacency lists store direction naturally: v is in u's list only for an edge u to v.

q: Directed edges are stored in a dict of lists. What does this print?
options: KeyError: 'b'
why: Each edge u to v is stored only in u's list. b has no outgoing edges, so get returns the default []. a has edges to b and c, so its list has 2 entries. Edges into b are not in b's list.
wrong: Those are the nodes with edges into b. Only outgoing edges are stored in a node's list.
b's list has no incoming edges, and a has two outgoing edges, not three.
get() returns the default when a key is missing; only graph['b'] would raise.

q: Why does DFS on a general graph need a visited set, while walking a tree from its root does not?
options: The visited set keeps the output in sorted order
It is needed only for weighted graphs, to remember distances
Graphs can have cycles and several paths to one node
It makes DFS run in O(log n) instead of O(n)
why: Without a visited set, DFS can go around a cycle forever or explore the same node many times. From the root of a tree, each node is reached by exactly one path, so nothing repeats.
wrong: It only records which nodes were seen; it does not order them.
Cycles break traversal whether or not edges have weights.
DFS is O(V + E) with the set. Without it, it may never finish.

q: Cities are connected by roads with travel times; most roads are two-way. How should an adjacency list store this?
options: Each city stores one weight, and its roads use that value
A two-way road is stored once, in the list of just one of its two cities
Weighted graphs need an adjacency matrix
Entries are (neighbour, time) pairs; a two-way road goes in both lists
why: A weight belongs to an edge, so it is stored with the neighbour. A two-way road is two directed edges, so it goes in both lists and can be found from either city.
wrong: Travel time belongs to a road, and roads from the same city differ.
Then the road cannot be found from the other city without scanning every list.
A list stores weights fine as (neighbour, weight) pairs.

q: A service reads a stream of user ids and must tell, for each id, whether it has appeared before. Which structure fits?
options: A list, checking membership with a scan
A hash set, with O(1) average checks
A sorted array with binary search
A stack of the ids seen so far
why: Only membership is needed, with no order and no counts. A hash set answers it directly and grows with the number of distinct ids.
wrong: Each scan is O(n), so the stream as a whole costs O(n^2).
The check is O(log n), but each new id must be inserted in place, which shifts O(n) items.
A stack exposes only its top, so checking older ids means popping through it.

q: A scheduler receives thousands of tasks per second, each with a priority, and must always run the highest-priority task next. Which structure fits?
options: A sorted array, with the highest priority at the end
A max-heap, used as a priority queue
A hash map from priority to task
A FIFO queue of tasks
why: The scheduler only ever needs the current maximum, while new tasks keep arriving. A heap gives the top in O(1) and insert and remove in O(log n), with no need to keep everything sorted.
wrong: Taking the top is O(1), but each insert shifts items to keep the order, which is O(n).
A hash map has no fast way to find the largest key.
A queue runs tasks in arrival order and ignores their priorities.

q: A sensor sends readings constantly, and the app must keep only the latest 100,000, dropping the oldest when a new one arrives. Which structure fits?
options: A deque or a ring buffer of that size
A stack, popping when it passes 100,000 readings
A dynamic array, removing index 0 when it passes 100,000
A hash set of readings
why: The pattern is first in, first out with a fixed size. A deque or ring buffer adds and drops at the two ends in O(1) and keeps the readings in arrival order.
wrong: A stack pops the newest reading, but the oldest one is the one to drop.
Correct result, but each removal at index 0 shifts every other reading.
A set loses arrival order and merges equal readings into one.

q: An LRU cache needs get and put in O(1) and evicts the least recently used entry when full. Why is the usual design a hash map plus a doubly linked list?
options: The map finds each node in O(1); the list moves or evicts it in O(1)
A hash map alone is enough, since it already keeps track of access order
A singly linked list would do the same job with less memory
A min-heap keyed by last use finds the oldest entry
why: The list keeps entries in recency order: a used node moves to the front and eviction removes the tail. Both are O(1) only with prev pointers and a direct reference to the node, which the map supplies.
wrong: A plain hash map does not track recency, so finding the oldest entry means scanning all of them.
Unlinking a node from the middle needs its predecessor, which a singly linked list finds only in O(n).
Every get changes a key's last use, and updating it in a heap costs O(log n) after an O(n) search.
